source_read: PMC author manuscript PMC8655458 (NIHMS1754902; final edited form Nat Rev Dis Primers 2021;7(1):16), a narrative Primer. Read in full in the built-in browser in my own tab on 2026-10-31: all sections, Tables 1-3, Boxes 1-4 and figure legends. get_page_text stopped at 120,000 characters partway through reference 103, so I read the rest of the reference list with javascript_tool on the same tab. Figure images not inspected; no correction is linked on the PMC page. All figures in it are cited second-hand (narrative review).

claims.overstatement: None: the claim reports the review's statement as second-hand and gives its two sources.
claims.note: Of the two sources Connor cites for the 90% (refs 189, 190), ref 190 is Sorensen et al. 2017, the claim's own primary source, and ref 189 is a 2019 BMJ clinical review (Chocron, Zuber & Vaucher). Connor's figure therefore adds no independent evidence and should not count towards 'replicated'. Connor's single 90% also merges two features that Sorensen reports separately (relief with hot bathing; relief after stopping). Connor also says almost all patients with the syndrome are heavy weekly users (not in the claim; consistent with Sorensen's weekly-use share) and, in the Quality of life section, that case series suggest heavy smoking 'can result in' the syndrome, a causal wording on case-series evidence. Connor calls it 'cannabis hyperemesis syndrome'.

anchors.locator: Diagnosis, screening and prevention > Differential diagnosis, 3rd paragraph; References 188-190
anchors.extracted: Recurrent vomiting is described as a symptom of cannabis hyperemesis syndrome, reported in emergency patients with cyclical vomiting and current or recent cannabis use (ref. 188, Simonetto et al. 2012, case series of 98). The differential diagnosis from other cyclical vomiting disorders is called underdeveloped because symptoms are poorly specified and overlap. Almost all patients are said to be heavy weekly users, and 90% to report that hot baths and abstinence relieve symptoms, citing refs 189 (Chocron et al. 2019, BMJ) and 190 (Sorensen et al. 2017).

Case series are said to suggest that heavy cannabis smoking can result in hyperemesis syndrome (refs 188, Simonetto 2012; 238, Bhandari et al. 2019, cyclic vomiting hospitalizations in Colorado). Evidence type: case series; no frequencies given.

claims.overstatement: None. The claim softens Connor's causal wording ('initiation before 16 years of age increases the risk') to 'linked to', which is appropriate for second-hand observational figures. The claim correctly flags Connor's arithmetic: 9.7% is about 1 in 10.3, while 'almost 1 in 19' would be about 5.3% (recomputed).
claims.note: All the figures attributed to Connor are found, with the citations the claim names: ref 45 is Cougle et al. 2016 (J Clin Psychiatry; NESARC, concurrent and prospective analyses of regular users); refs 15 and 31 are the 'two reviews' for 30-40% (Budney, Sofis & Borodovsky 2019, a review with policy commentary; Coffey & Patton 2016, a review of findings from one Australian cohort, the Victorian Adolescent Health Cohort Study); ref 1 is the UN World Drug Report 2020 for 'as many as one-third' of daily users; refs 39-41 are the three sources for first use before 16 (Butterworth et al., 2007 Australian national survey; Le Strat et al. 2015, US; Behrendt et al. 2009); refs 37, 42 and 43 support early onset (a book chapter, a genetics review, a twin meta-analysis). Connor gives no definitions, measures or adjustment for any of these figures. Omission in the claim: the same sentence that gives one-third for daily use also gives 'approximately 1 in 10 regular users' (UN report), a frequency figure on yet another denominator. Consistent with the claim: Connor lists negative life events as independent predictors of incident use disorder, citing van der Pol et al. 2013; and it calls the lack of measures of THC consumed a major limitation of epidemiological research, where only frequency is usually assessed.

anchors.extracted: Risk of progression from use to use disorder said to increase with frequency of use (no citation). About 17.0% of people smoking weekly and 19.0% of those smoking daily met criteria for dependence; in a longitudinal study 9.7% of weekly users without dependence progressed to dependence within a year, which the review calls 'almost 1 in 19'; both cited to Cougle et al. 2016 (NESARC). No definition or adjustment given.

Lifetime risk of dependence said to rise to 30-40% among people with a history of daily use, citing Budney et al. 2019 (review and commentary) and Coffey & Patton 2016 (review of one cohort's findings).

anchors.locator: Introduction (unheaded, after the Abstract), 2nd paragraph; Reference 1
anchors.extracted: Use disorder said to occur in about 1 in 10 regular users and in as many as one-third of people who use daily, citing the UN World Drug Report 2020; denominator of 'regular' not defined.

anchors.locator: Epidemiology > Age of onset, 1st paragraph; References 37, 39-43
anchors.extracted: Starting before 16 is said to increase the risk of use disorder, the rate of progression to it, other substance use disorders and anxiety disorders (three sources, refs 39-41). Twin studies are said to show that earlier onset is influenced by genetic factors even after accounting for other substance use, conduct disorder, depression and anxiety (ref. 42). Common genetic or shared environmental factors, including social and developmental vulnerability, are said to contribute to early onset (refs 37, 42, 43). Median age of onset is given as 18-19 years and the mean as 15-16 (refs 37, 38).

anchors.locator: Mechanisms/pathophysiology > Aetiology > Risk and protective factors, 1st paragraph; Reference 164
anchors.extracted: Number and type of negative life events described as independent predictors of incident use disorder, citing van der Pol et al. 2013 (3-year prospective study of frequent use).
The absence of adequate measures of the amount of THC consumed is called a major limitation of epidemiological research; usually only frequency of use is assessed.

claims.overstatement: Not an overstatement but an incomplete description of how this review uses 'about 1 in 10'. The claim says the reviews' 'about 9 in 100, or about 1 in 10' is cited to the US surveys or matches them, and for Connor names the 1990-92 survey. That is true of the 9% in Epidemiology > Prevalence. But Connor's abstract says the use disorder affects about 10% of the 193 million people worldwide who use cannabis, and its introduction says it occurs in about 1 in 10 'regular users'. Both cite the UN World Drug Report and use denominators (people who used in the past year worldwide; regular users) that do not match the surveys' denominator (anyone who had ever used).
claims.note: Supported parts: the 9% and its comparison figures (tobacco 32%, heroin 23%, cocaine 17%, alcohol 15%), cited to ref. 30 (Anthony, Warner & Kessler 1994, the NCS). Connor dates the estimate 'in 1992'; the fieldwork ran 1990-92 and the paper appeared in 1994. DSM-5 use disorder needs 2 of 11 criteria with marked clinical impairment or distress over 12 months, with severity graded mild (2-3), moderate (4-5) and severe (6+). About 30% of people who use cannabis may develop a use disorder in recent US national data, cited to Hasin et al. 2015 (ref. 32); Connor gives neither the measure nor the denominator (it does not say past-year use) and suggests the rise may reflect potency, legal status and acceptance. 'Narrower' (DSM-III-R and DSM-IV dependence against DSM-5 use disorder) is the editors' inference. Connor supports it: DSM-5 merged abuse and dependence on evidence of a single severity dimension, and Table 1 marks 7 of the 11 DSM-5 criteria as DSM-IV-TR dependence criteria. Connor does not state the DSM-IV threshold. Internal inconsistency: 193 million (abstract) against 192 million (introduction and Prevalence) people using in the past year.

anchors.extracted: Lifetime risk of dependence among people who had ever tried cannabis estimated 'in 1992' at 9%, lower than tobacco (32%), heroin (23%), cocaine (17%) and alcohol (15%), citing Anthony, Warner & Kessler 1994 (National Comorbidity Survey). Same paragraph: about 30% of people who use cannabis may develop a use disorder in more recent nationally representative US data (ref. 32, Hasin et al. 2015), with no measure or denominator given; possibly reflecting potency, legal status and societal acceptance.

anchors.locator: Diagnosis, screening and prevention > Diagnostic systems, 2nd paragraph; Table 1 and its notes
anchors.extracted: DSM-5 replaced cannabis abuse and dependence with one use-disorder category (abuse and dependence symptoms on a single severity dimension). Diagnosis needs 2 of 11 symptoms causing marked clinical impairment or distress over the past 12 months; 2-3 symptoms mild, 4-5 moderate, 6 or more severe. Table 1 marks 7 of the 11 criteria as DSM-IV-TR dependence criteria; ICD-11 dependence is described as similar to DSM-IV-TR dependence.

anchors.locator: Abstract; Introduction (unheaded, after the Abstract), 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Reference 1
anchors.extracted: Use disorder said to affect about 10% of the 193 million people who use cannabis worldwide (abstract); 192 million used in 2018 and 9.9% of past-year users used daily or near daily (introduction, 1st paragraph); about 1 in 10 'regular users' and as many as one-third of daily users have a use disorder (2nd paragraph). All cited to the UN World Drug Report 2020, on past-year or 'regular' denominators rather than ever use.

claims.overstatement: The statements attributed to Connor alone, or with Curran, are faithful: the time course, and no serious risk with usually only supportive care when there are no medical or psychiatric comorbidities, which the claim words as 'described as'. The DSM-5 definition, attributed to Bahji and Connor together, differs from Connor's account in two ways. (1) Connor has the signs occurring within 1 week of cessation; it does not mention cutting down, so 'stopping or cutting down' is not supported by this source. (2) Connor includes the requirement that the signs cause clinically severe distress or impairment (Connor's wording), which the claim leaves out. Both widen the definition. The outcome definition counts as an error, not wording, under this round's brief.
claims.note: Connor's time course (begin 24-48 h after cessation, peak within the first week, last 1-2 weeks) is itself second-hand, from Budney et al. 2003 (ref. 176), as the claim's 'second-hand' says. Qualifier for the claim's prevalence figures: Connor repeats Bahji's 17%, 54% and 87% (ref. 203, with Livne 2019, ref. 177) but relabels them. It calls them the prevalence 'in the general population of cannabis users' (12-17%) and the share of treatment-seeking patients with use disorder who report 'clinically severe' withdrawal (54% of outpatients, 87% of inpatients). Connor should not be cited for those figures. Its 12% for frequent users with DSM-5 withdrawal in the past year (Livne 2019) matches the claim's 12.1% from Bahji. Also consistent with the claim: tobacco co-use is linked to more withdrawal symptoms (ref. 46, a systematic review), and CB1 agonists (dronabinol, nabilone, nabiximols) reduced withdrawal intensity. Connor notes that many withdrawal symptoms also occur in other substances' withdrawal and in other mental disorders. In the editors' wording, 'no serious risk' is used only as Connor's statement, with its stated condition; good.

anchors.locator: Diagnosis, screening and prevention > Diagnostic systems, 3rd paragraph; References 4, 176, 177
anchors.extracted: DSM-5 withdrawal: three or more of these within 1 week of cessation: irritability, anger or aggression; nervousness or anxiety; sleep difficulty (insomnia, disturbing dreams); decreased appetite or weight loss; restlessness; depressed mood; and at least one physical symptom causing severe discomfort (abdominal pain, shakiness or tremors, sweating, fever, chills or headache). The signs must also cause clinically severe distress or impairment (Connor's wording). Symptoms typically begin 24-48 hours after cessation, peak within the first week and last 1-2 weeks (ref. 176, Budney et al. 2003). In a nationally representative US sample, 12% of people who used frequently had DSM-5 withdrawal in the past 12 months (ref. 177, Livne et al. 2019). Many symptoms also occur in other withdrawal syndromes and mental disorders.

Without medical or psychiatric comorbidities, withdrawal is said not to pose serious risks, and most people with use disorder need only supportive care (no citation for this sentence). Behavioural management includes psychoeducation about expected symptoms and time course, and coping skills (ref. 206).

Prevalence 'in the general population of cannabis users' given as 12-17%; '54% of outpatients and 87% of inpatients' with use disorder seeking treatment said to report clinically severe withdrawal; cited to Livne 2019 and Bahji 2020. The labels differ from Bahji's populations and outcome as the claim reports them (people with regular use or use disorder; withdrawal as each study defined it). Withdrawal is said to make quitting harder and may precipitate relapse.

anchors.locator: Mechanisms/pathophysiology > Endocannabinoids and the reward system, 6th paragraph; Epidemiology > Consumption patterns, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Withdrawal intensity reduced by CB1 agonists (dronabinol, nabilone; nabiximols, about 1:1 THC:CBD), refs 93, 95, 96. Tobacco co-use is associated with more withdrawal symptoms and higher risk of use disorder (ref. 46, Peters et al. 2012).

key_findings.note: Second-hand status and the ref. 30/15/31/32 identities checked against the reference list. The Leung et al. (2020) comparison in the note comes from another card and was not checked.
Ref. 34 is Dilley et al. 2019, 'Prevalence of cannabis use in youths after legalization in Washington state' (JAMA Pediatrics), as the note says.

Content and locators right. Two fidelity points: (1) the Primer prints 'clinically severe distress or impairment' and 'severe discomfort', whereas the card writes 'clinically significant' (DSM-5's own word, not the Primer's); (2) the card reproduces without comment the Primer's labels for Bahji's figures ('general population of cannabis users'; treatment-seeking patients with CUD reporting 'clinically severe' withdrawal), which do not match the population named in ref. 203's title (people with regular or dependent use). See missed.
The note's comparison with Murray et al. (2016) comes from another card and was not checked.
Ref. 233's title (Eisen et al. 2002: self-reported health measures, socio-demographics and quality of life; monozygotic co-twin study in men) confirms the note.

Found independently in step 1. Ref. 188's title is 'Cannabinoid hyperemesis: a case series of 98 patients'. Not noted on the card: one of the two sources for the 90% (ref. 190) is Sorensen et al. 2017, read in this round, so the Primer's figure is not independent of it.

The Pasman facts in the note (three data sources, one the 16-cohort ICC; 8 independent genome-wide significant variants; SNP heritability 11%; instruments explaining 0.15% to 1.12%) match my own reading of Pasman et al. 2018 in this round.
Table 3 rows checked (nabilone, dronabinol, nabiximols, FAAH inhibitor, etc.).

Ref. 120 (pages 461-369) and ref. 239 ('Caulk ins') are confirmed. Ref. 246 does print a volume and pages ('Psychol. Med. 48, 2346-2352'); only the year is missing. Correction: 'ref 246 has no year' (not 'no year or volume').

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' narrative-review checklist; overall high from the absence of a systematic search, with the overall no less severe than the worst domain. I did not recount the 47 of 326 references with a Primer author.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor. The Primer is mostly hedged; the main stretches are those the card lists. I would add the relabelling of Bahji's withdrawal figures (see missed).

missed: Management > Cannabis withdrawal, 1st paragraph: the Primer gives Bahji et al.'s pooled figures (ref. 203) as the prevalence 'in the general population of cannabis users' (12-17%) and as the share of treatment-seeking patients with CUD reporting 'clinically severe' withdrawal (54% of outpatients, 87% of inpatients). By ref. 203's own title the samples are people with regular or dependent use, and nothing in the Primer shows the outcome was restricted to clinically severe withdrawal. Claims should take these figures from Bahji, not from the Primer's description. Suggested reporting issue.

Diagnosis, screening and prevention > Diagnostic systems, 3rd paragraph: the Primer's account of DSM-5 withdrawal has the signs occurring within 1 week of 'cessation' (no reduction), requires 'clinically severe distress or impairment' and describes the physical symptom as causing 'severe discomfort'. 'Severe' is stronger than 'clinically significant', the DSM-5 wording that the card itself uses. Quote the criteria from DSM-5, not from the Primer. Minor reporting issue.

Diagnosis, screening and prevention > Differential diagnosis, 3rd paragraph: of the two sources cited for '90% report that hot baths and abstinence relieve their symptoms', ref. 190 is Sorensen et al. 2017 (the primary source of the CHS claim, read in this round) and ref. 189 is a 2019 BMJ clinical review. The Primer's figure is therefore not independent support, and it merges two features that Sorensen reports separately.
